report.source_text: She was started on verapamil 40 mg every 8 hours on arrival; on hospital day 3 her dose was increased to 60 mg every 8 hours due to sustained frequent ectopic beats. On day 4, she continued to have premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) but with a decrease in frequency. The paediatric cardiology electrophysiologist evaluated the patient at bedside and cleared her for discharge. She was instructed to continue verapamil at home, to follow-up with paediatric cardiology in 2 weeks and a Holter monitor was ordered. Additionally, she was advised to avoid vigorous physical activity for 4 weeks.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 8-year-old girl presented to the ED with lightheadedness, presyncope, and documented ventricular tachycardia by EMS. The initial ECG showed a monomorphic accelerated ventricular rhythm with left bundle branch block morphology. Initial blood tests including troponin, electrolytes, and chest radiograph were unremarkable. On hospital day 2, cardiac MRI demonstrated right ventricular free wall contusion with focal delayed enhancement, edema, regional wall motion abnormalities involving the right ventricular outflow tract, a subacute precordial hematoma extending from the great vessels anterior to the pulmonary artery and RV outflow tract, and a small pericardial effusion possibly with pericardial hematoma. The patient was treated with verapamil, which reduced the frequency of premature ventricular contractions. Follow-up Holter monitoring up to two months post-event showed persistent monomorphic PVCs at 26%-27% burden with occasional couplets. The pediatric cardiology electrophysiologist cleared her for discharge with activity restrictions and outpatient follow-up.
